transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-10-05 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Donovan (Lakeshore Head of ML), Elena Cruz (Lakeshore SRE), Tom Wu (Lakeshore Security)

Summary: quick run through of last week's benchmarks, digging into Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) regressions when switching to streaming, sequence length impacts, and kernel selection guidance.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick recap — we ran the mixed workload benchmark last Wednesday, priya sent over the raw logs.
[00:18] Priya Nair: yeah, hi. we saw average TTFT at ~72ms for hosted v1 but when we flip streaming on it jumps to ~120ms for the same model, i'm guessing it's the extra socket handshake + chunking overhead, also our kernel choice default is the fused attention kernel which performs differently at short sequences.
[00:35] Mark Donovan: right that's the number we were worried about, end users notice that first token pause. our SLO is 100ms for first token.
[00:46] Elena Cruz: and we also saw p95 tail spikes during traffic bursts, like up to 380ms. that's on the dedicated pool, right?
[00:55] Priya Nair: correct, dedicated. though the dedicated config had smaller batch sizes. I think two levers: streaming socket tuning and kernel choice for our sequence length profile.
[01:10] Tom Wu: quick sec — from security perspective, if we're moving to dedicated we need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs retention. also curious if streaming increases our surface area.
[01:22] Jordan Lee: good point, we'll share SOC2 docs and the KMS integration note after the call. streaming itself doesn't change encryption at rest, it's transport — but we'll document the TLS endpoints and mutual TLS options.
[01:34] Mark Donovan: back to latency — we sent over the sequence-length histogram. most of our calls are between 32 and 128 tokens, but there is a tail to 512. that tail might be causing kernel fallback to slower paths.
[01:50] Priya Nair: yes, when the runtime sees frequent long sequences it sometimes picks the general-purpose kernel instead of the short-seq-optimized kernel. also quantization choices matter: 4-bit QAT path has different kernel availability.
[02:05] Jordan Lee: can you walk us through the exact benchmark config? priya, you mentioned 1k requests?
[02:12] Priya Nair: we did a 300-sample run first — I'll run the 1k synthetic workload hitting the Dedicated pool, replicating production sequence-length mix Mark gave. We'll capture TTFT, token-per-second, p95/p99 for both streaming and non-streaming modes.
[02:27] Mark Donovan: we want to see TTFT delta, and also the effect if you enable prefix/KV cache — our flows reuse context a lot.
[02:35] Priya Nair: good call, I'll run three variants: cold (no cache), warm (KV cache enabled), streaming enabled/disabled.
[02:44] Elena Cruz: for the streaming case please make sure chunk size is 256 bytes and keep-alive socket settings match our infra, otherwise numbers don't transfer.
[02:54] Priya Nair: noted.
[02:57] Jordan Lee: about kernel choices — our runtime logs which kernel was selected per request, priya will attach a kernel selection trace. if we see frequent slow kernels for 32-128 token requests, we can force the short-seq kernel via a runtime flag or a model variant compiled with the short-optim kernel.
[03:14] Mark Donovan: is forcing kernel safe? will it regress accuracy or cause any numerical differences?
[03:21] Priya Nair: in our tests it's a pure execution kernel swap, no functional change. quantization plus kernel can change minor last-digit numeric differences but nothing that affects outputs in our evals. still we'll run regen tests.
[03:33] Tom Wu: any difference in memory or KV cache behaviour?
[03:36] Priya Nair: short-seq kernels often are more memory-friendly for per-token computation; and if we keep KV cache pinned in GPU memory it reduces recompute. biggest memory delta shows up with very long sequences.
[03:48] Mark Donovan: we also asked about batching — our traffic is bursty, how aggressively will Redwood batch? aggressive batching helps throughput but hurts TTFT.
[03:57] Jordan Lee: we can set per-route SLOs and batching policy. for Lakeshore we'd recommend conservative batching for low-latency routes (max batch size 4, batch timeout 10ms) and larger batch for background jobs.
[04:10] Elena Cruz: can that be done per-route? we have fraud alerts route that must be <100ms and an analytics route that's fine at 1s.
[04:16] Jordan Lee: yup per-route and per-model. also autoscale to add more workers under load so batching doesn't accumulate.
[04:24] Priya Nair: one anomaly we saw: when streaming is enabled, network TLS renegotiation for short-lived connections bumped the first-byte time. switching to persistent connections/keep-alive and tuning Nagle settings dropped TTFT by ~30ms in our test.
[04:40] Mark Donovan: can you replicate that with our infra keep-alive config?
[04:44] Priya Nair: yes, Elena's config note will help.
[04:47] Tom Wu: security again — what about audit logs for streaming sessions? will each chunk be logged?
[04:52] Jordan Lee: only request/response metadata and high-level streaming events are logged by default; payload logging is opt-in and can be disabled for PII. we'll send the audit log linkage doc.
[05:03] Mark Donovan: good. what's the plan and timeline?
[05:06] Jordan Lee: plan: Priya runs 1k benchmark (three variants) by Oct 12, collects kernel traces and TTFT/p95/p99. Jordan will send kernel tuning doc and streaming guide by Oct 8. Mark to provide updated histograms by Oct 7. After we have results, schedule canary demo for week of Oct 18.
[05:25] Priya Nair: I'll also instrument per-token timing to confirm where the time is spent — e.g., SSL, accept, chunking, kernel compute.
[05:33] Elena Cruz: i'll check VPC peering windows and share the maintenance window.
[05:37] Tom Wu: i'll review KMS integration and confirm any customer-side key policies.
[05:41] Jordan Lee: great. any other questions?
[05:44] Mark Donovan: one more—if we switch to the short-seq compiled model variant, what's the rollout path? can we do canary?
[05:51] Priya Nair: yes canary supported — we can route X% of traffic to the short-seq variant and monitor accuracy/regressions. automatic fallback to the original model if errors cross threshold.
[06:02] Mark Donovan: perfect. thanks everyone.
[06:05] Jordan Lee: thanks — we'll follow up with the docs and benchmark results.

Action items (recap):
- Priya to run benchmarks (1k) and attach kernel selection traces.
- Jordan to send kernel tuning + streaming guide.
- Mark to provide seq-length histogram and production mix.
- Elena to confirm VPC/peering maintenance window.
- Tom to validate KMS policies.

Links shared during call: 
- benchmark logs (s3://lakeshore/poc/benchmarks/oct05/raw_logs) (placeholder)
- kernel tuning guide (will be shared post-call)
- SOC2 and KMS integration note (will be shared post-call)

End of transcript.
